title: OpenAI aids NATO and allied cyber defense: up to 300 billion tokens a month, 95% of 88 issues confirmed
summary: Cyber defense teams review large volumes of software and investigate suspicious activity every day. OpenAI says it is putting security models into the hands of NATO and several European countries through Daybreak, helping defenders find vulnerabilities faster while humans still confirm and fix them.
ai_summary: OpenAI is providing cybersecurity models through Daybreak to NATO's core institutions, with access already extended to the EU, France, Germany, Poland, and Ukraine. NATO has used up to 300 billion input and output tokens per month. On results: ENISA found four vulnerabilities and all were fixed; in a November joint report from ENISA and CERT-EU, maintainers reviewed 88 potential issues and confirmed 95% as genuine; CERT Polska found six MikroTik RouterOS vulnerabilities and the vendor has fixed them. For defenders, the value is faster initial triage and vulnerability exploration, with humans keeping oversight and final judgment. The biggest limitation: the announcement does not disclose pricing, contracts, or costs, and does not say whether the 300 billion tokens is a steady run rate or a peak.
brief: NATO has used up to 300 billion input and output tokens per month.
ENISA used the models to find four vulnerabilities, all fixed.
A November report reviewed 88 potential issues and confirmed 95% as genuine.
CERT Polska found six MikroTik RouterOS vulnerabilities, and the vendor has shipped fixes.

sections.h: What it is: OpenAI hands Daybreak to government and military defenders

blocks.p: On November 17, 2026, OpenAI announced a partnership with NATO Communications and Information Agency (NCIA) to provide Daybreak cybersecurity models to NATO's core institutions, helping protect member networks.

Daybreak is an AI tool for "trusted defenders" doing authorized security work: reviewing software, investigating suspicious activity, validating vulnerabilities, and developing and testing fixes. Its target users are government and national cyber agencies, not a general-purpose chat product.

sections.h: How much NATO uses: up to 300 billion tokens a month

blocks.p: The announcement gives one scale number: NATO has used up to 300 billion input and output tokens per month on this work. Tokens are the smallest unit of text a model reads and generates, and 300 billion reflects a large accumulated throughput of code review, alert triage, and vulnerability analysis.

Note the "up to" qualifier: this is a peak figure, not a fixed monthly amount, and the announcement does not give an average. Vendors usually cite usage figures to show scale, not to claim every month hits the ceiling.

sections.h: What role AI plays in exercises: faster triage, not replacing humans

blocks.p: OpenAI also supported the 2026 Crossed Swords exercise, organized by the NATO Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence (CCDCOE). The exercise included a new training stream in which participants built, deployed, and evaluated AI agents for cyber operations using OpenAI Daybreak in the technical environment.

The key element is human oversight. The announcement says participants acted as operators of AI agents and emphasizes maintaining human oversight. AI provides speed and scale; people still make the final judgment.

sections.h: Allied results: 4 vulnerabilities fixed, 88 issues 95% genuine

blocks.p: Beyond NATO, OpenAI has provided these cyber models to defenders in Europe, including the EU's cybersecurity agency ENISA and national cyber agencies in France (ANSSI), Germany, and Poland. Ukraine's Ministry of Digital Transformation is also using Daybreak to protect civilian infrastructure.

blocks.p: ENISA used these models to find four vulnerabilities in software used across EU institutions, and fixes have been published for all four, with links listed in the announcement.

More notable is the November joint report from ENISA and CERT-EU, the EU institutions' computer emergency response team. They reviewed 27 software projects using frontier models, including OpenAI models accessed through Daybreak, along with tools including the Codex security plug-in. Software maintainers reviewed 88 potential issues, and 95% were confirmed as genuine.

callout.title: What the 95% actually means
callout.text: The announcement says 95% is the aggregate result "across the models tested", not OpenAI's number alone. It means that of the issues AI flagged and humans confirmed, 95% turned out to be genuine. That shows AI triage can save a lot of work, but human maintainers still do the final confirmation.

sections.h: The CERT Polska MikroTik case: six vulnerabilities, vendor fixed

blocks.p: Poland's CERT Polska used OpenAI models to help find six vulnerabilities in MikroTik RouterOS and coordinated disclosure with the vendor. Researchers directed the work, tested findings on real systems, and verified their impact; AI accelerated vulnerability analysis and exploration.
MikroTik then released fixes, and CERT Polska confirmed the fixes blocked the attacks it had observed. For network operators using affected devices, that offers a concrete remediation path.

sections.h: Cost and pricing: no numbers published

blocks.p: The announcement gives no prices, contract amounts, or per-token costs. In a statement, NCIA General Manager Dylan Browne said that as they scale adoption, they will build a deeper understanding of token consumption, usage patterns, and the economics of AI models, to optimize costs, evaluate competing solutions, and make procurement decisions.

In other words, the organization is itself working through the economics but has not published specific figures. If you want to know how much Daybreak costs or how it is billed, there is no public answer yet.

list: Price and cost: no per-token, per-project, or contract figures.
Whether NATO's 300 billion tokens is a steady run rate or a one-month peak: the announcement only says "up to", with no average.
What model Daybreak actually is, its context window, and what access controls it has: not detailed.
Specific results for Ukraine: the announcement only says it helps identify and fix vulnerabilities faster, with no numbers.
Whether these tools are open to ordinary businesses or individuals, or how to apply: not stated.

blocks.p: The value is clear: for national cyber agencies and multinational defense teams handling huge volumes of code and alerts every day, AI speeds up initial triage — flagging suspicious code and potential vulnerabilities before handing them to humans. The three results in the announcement follow the same pattern of AI triage plus human confirmation: four vulnerabilities fixed, 88 issues with 95% confirmed genuine, and six MikroTik vulnerabilities fixed.

The costs are also clear: it consumes a lot of tokens, up to 300 billion per month for NATO, which means real compute budget; and it still depends on experienced researchers and maintainers. AI cannot publish fixes on its own.

list: If you run a national cyber agency or multinational defense team: Daybreak is a good fit for initial triage and acceleration in authorized security work, but pair it with a solid human review process.
If you maintain software: every AI-reported issue still needs to be verified one by one. A 95% confirmation rate saves effort, but it is not zero false positives.
If you are a regular enterprise security team: this post does not explain how to get access, so do not assume you can use it directly; watch for future application and pricing details.
